This doesn't really have anything to do with GLM-5.3. This is what happens when you share models between users and don't do your bookkeeping properly, the actual model doesn't matter. What it shows is that there isn't enough isolation between the user sessions and that memory can overlap when that should never be possible.

This is an SGLANG and a Cloudflare bug long before it is a Z.AI model bug, I don't see what they could have done about it. Cloudflare should own it instead of naming other (imo innocent) parties in the title.

At no point do we claim that it is a bug with the model. We specifically outline how it was a mis-configuration on Cloudflare's part and a bug in SGLang. We name the model in the title because our customers need to know which of our endpoints was affected. In fact, we say "the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model", not "GLM-5.3".

Not buying that. You explicitly mention the model name in the title the 'GLM 5.3 workers AI model' suggests it is something specific to GLM 5.3 which it is not. You mention Sglang and are all surprised that it didn't throw an error. But the issue was yours all along.

Yeah, their title is absolutely implying a GLM bug to anyone who doesn't read it super closely.

There's a huge amount of unnecessary extraneous details in the headline that distract from "this is a Cloudflare bug".

Not sure if the title was edited but as is it is very clear to me this is a bug on their side and I have no idea how a technically literate person (someone using the model via cloudflare?) who would misinterpret given the reference to the cache.

The title is poorly worded. I can easily see how it can be conflated in passing. Naming the model is silly in the title. It should be mentioned in the article but as read the title suggests it’s something related to this model.

I have read this post, and it appears that this is indeed an issue specific to the GLM 5.3 model on their platform. I am unsure whether this is because only GLM 5.3 uses SGLang or because only its configuration is problematic.

Did we read different articles? None of the issues they brought up (architecture splitting, memory transport, Cloudflare's misconfigured context window provisioning, the SGLang state leak, lack of client error provisioning) are model related. These all exist at the layer of the harness (ie Cloudflare's configuration).

A better title would be "Cross-request KV cache exposure in Cloudflare provisioned GLM-5.3 Workers AI model" because it narrows culpability. Just posting it on the Cloudflare blog isn't enough for that in the age of AI and SEO data-scrapes and it'd be surprising to me if the authors didn't know that.
The issue is not with this model; rather, it affects only this model.
They could have removed GLM 5.3 from the title, and the title and the body would still make perfect sense.
I think it's in the title because it's also doing double-duty of informing customers that only usage of the GLM-5.3 model was potentially impacted. I agree that it's so what confusing, though.

I was surprised in reading the article that it had nothing to do with the contents of the model.  It could have been any model capable of 1M context that triggered this bug/misconfig on Cloudflare/SGLangs side.  The title is extremely misleading.
Changing "model" to "endpoint" might help since it's the endpoint, not the model

> We name the model in the title because our customers need to know which of our endpoints was affected

Then you would used "endpoint" instead of "model". In fact, there's actually zero reasons to put any model or endpoint in the title if the bug is yours alone.

You should change the title.

Most people will read this headline and assume Cloudflare is intentionally trying to squash open-weight models. Given how superfluous the model is to the content, it's easy to believe that narrative.

If that wasn't your intent, you really ought to change the title ASAP. Time is ticking before tech journalists and social media decide to run with that narrative and make your public relations department sad.

What's the point of even mentioning GLM-5.3? That's a detail that only belongs in the body.

Did you ever given any thought about how confusing the title may be?

Did AI write this title and you just use it without ever wondering if it makes sense at all?

"Cross-request KV cache exposure in X model".

Which part of that is not claiming the exposure is in X model? Cloudflare is stopping to be cool, this is the start. I guess, cf is now big enough for enshitification to start.
Then remove GLM-5.3 from the title.
Not what I am seeing. not sure if there is A/B testing here.
Their AI won’t let them
To me it's obvious that anything related to caching has little to do with the model itself. And it's nice to know from the title that you could only be affected if you used this model.

It took me until "We have remediated the issue" to realize Cloudflare is talking about an issue they have in their infrastructure, up until that point they're not making that clear at all, and seems to point towards something else, unless you of course already are aware of what exact names Cloudflare uses for their products...

It does have to do with GLM-5.3 but you're correct it doesn't have anything to do with the model.

It effects the _endpoint serving GLM-5.3_

I'm not sure how else you'd identify the GLM-5.3 serving endpoint without naming GLM-5.3.

That said, having the word "model" in the title is misleading imo

It seems like you're trying to imply this was an intentional bias due to the nationality of the model authors. But the first sentence of the article is:

"On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026."

Meaning the issue was a cache exposure with the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model. If the title was, "Cache exposure issue with GLM-5.3," I would agree it's ambiguous and maybe intentionally harmful. But it literally says, "Workers AI model" which is clearly a Cloudflare product.

I did not mention anybody's nationality, nor did I imply that that was important.

Downthread I suggested "Cloudflare configuration error leaked data between user sessions" which I think is far better. You could improve on it further: "Cloudflare AI worker configuration error leaked data between user sessions". But this could have happened with any model.
Why are you bringing up people's nationalities? This seems incredibly inappropriate
Probably because there's an on-going conspiracy that's been all over HN that these large corporations are on a smear campaign against Chinese models.
You're the one perpetuating that.
Yes, because debunking something is equivalent to perpetuating it. Can't imply someone might be racist because then you perpetuate racism. That literally makes no sense lol.
You can't debunk that which isn't said.
It has been said, ad naesuem, all over HN for weeks now. I pegged the OP wrong.
You are a weirdo just making things up
What a quaint rebuttal.
You didn't even provide anything logical to rebute in the first place. So my comment was not a rebuttal, just an observation

I like this RCA a lot more than most. I appreciate the ownership and clear explanation of why their testing did not catch this bug.

Also impressed with the speed to address the issue unplug the model and then pretty quick remediation, the speed to remediation matters less to me, but good to see they can act quickly on their platform to kill the serving of the model.

"We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. "

Did they advertise it as 1,048,576 token when they only had room for 681,280 tokens?
Next sentence: "We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue."

Which is pointing the finger at Sglang, who also weren't responsible for this.

At a minimum someone should have realized during testing that their utilization figures are off by 40%.

A much better title would be "Cloudflare configuration error leaked data between user sessions"
I mean they are responsible for this. It's definitely a bug on their end.

Doesn't matter, they could have marketed it as 1 million token window, you would then infer, get to 600k and get an error.  You won't be able to finish your work, and you won't get credit for 600k tokens.
They thought it worked up to 1m token window

why would they think that?  I'm not a pro, but I know you can't serve more than kv cache pool that you have.  If you want to run concurrent requests, you need to have more kv cache pool than your context window.  The entire thing is weird, my bet is they were thinking most people will be using about 100k cache, compacting, etc and not nearing 600k ever.

See my other comment, this is likely only for the prefill GPU pool, a normal 1M token session would work fine. I think Cloudflare should probably link an explainer on how model serving works at the top of the post because a lot of people are not familiar at that level of detail.
Bro, I had to read this sentence in the context of the previous one, 3 fcking times.. and it sill does not make any sense to me.
Sounds like they are saying they tested with a long prompt and just tested for a failure, but the test likely would have seen that same KV cache leakage and just interpreted it as success.
thank you...

So they knowingly deployed a configuration with an overflow risk, much like writing code with a buffer overflow exploit.

They assumed that it wasn't like an overflow exploit, despite the fact that's exactly what they'd set up to happen, on the grounds of thinking the equivalent of, "oh this probably uses smart pointers, we'll be fine".

That's how I read it anyway.

I read that as you can only do a single prefill up to 681k tokens, separate from cache hit or generation. I think people try pretty hard to avoid a cache miss on sessions that long and rarely do standalone requests that big so the situation triggering this condition is rare. If you run a normal coding session with many turns it would get to 1M ok.

Shit happens, this is normal. However, this:

> We were aware of this mismatch before launch

Isn't normal. Am I misunderstanding or are they openly confessing they've stopped caring about quality at all? Why would you launch when you know it's wrong?
Maybe they forgot to run this one by the lawyers before posting. I'm surprised they'd publicly admit to that
Please consider to update the title in: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the AI model workers
Other providers probably don't even know/care that this is happening

Last year it happened to me more than once that dictating something in chatgpt would become a completely different message after processing, not in a misheard type of way but just a separate conversation more easily explained by the same type of KV cache issue here.

I think in the last year I've had it happen once where I seemingly got someone else's response, it was very odd. I rewound and got what I expected. It was correlated to Anthropic's roll out of new models at the time which always seems to cause instability in their apis.
Other providers might have better isolated KV stores?
I've had this happen with ChatGPT too.

(Some random internet user pasted me things that were clearly from my ChatGPT session, he identified me because it had links to my github).  So it wasn't a hallucination, it appeared to be some sort of KV cache leakage, though I obviously don't know the true root cause of the bug.

I wonder if the chatgpt shirtless guy is from the same kind of issue

What worries me is what was actually in those leaked prompts. This is a million-token context model, and people use that context to paste whole repos and configs, .env files included. So the realistic worst case isn't someone's chat text, it's someone's API keys. The write-up explains the root cause well, but doesn't say whether the customers whose prompts ended up in other people's responses were notified.
Even cloudflare being unable to deploy this technology correctly makes me think there are some serious failures of knowledge transmission happening somewhere between theoreticians and practicians.
cloudflare has never been known to deploy stable software especially for features early in their lifetime

A much better title for this would be something like "Cross-Tenant KV Cache Exposure in Shared LLM Inference: Analysis and Remediation". As others have pointed out there is no need to mention GLM-5.3 in the title. As someone that has been using GLM-5.3 I immediately thought there is a cause for concern here, only to find out there isn't.

Read this last night. I was completely thrown off when I read this line:

> We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue

Surely “we expected and error but got a successful response” merits investigating rather than moving on?

Reminds me of a bug I found in a very popular browser testing service that spun up iOS vm's/devices for on-device testing.

I copied the clipboard from the device, and my clipboard was full of another users credentials that they were obviously trying to paste into their own VM. Their devices were leaking clipboard data to each other.

I reported the vulnerability and asked if there was any bounty program (I wasn't looking for vulnerabilities but didn't hurt to ask), to which they said no, but they could send me a signed letter thanking me of my contributions. I said, great, thanks - and never heard back.

All pretty disappointing.
It seems more specific to the platform than the model. Maybe Cross-request KV cache exposure in the AI model workers would be a better fitting title?
Interesting. That might explain the few times I've received completely unrelated responses from a certain provider's API.
I'm just surprised more serverless providers haven't found (or publicly disclosed) similar issues, yet.

I kind of forgot about the shared tenancy attack model. I think I was assuming/hoping the software was magically isolating my tokens, when in reality that's impossible for shared tenants. There's whole classes of attacks on things like shared cache, before we get to the LLM-specific features and potential bugs. Enterprises with highly sensitive data should really be on non-shared hosts.

Six months ago I had a very basic prompt to Claude at work return very specific, unrelated information that looked very much like it could have come from someone else in the company. We raised an incident and were told by Anthropic (in a 100% Claude generated email) that this wasn't possible and that AI sometimes makes mistakes like that. I'm not sure how much they investigated but apparently their email was enough for legal and compliance so eh.
Upshot: even though sglang is written in Rust, they still got burned by undefined behavior from uninitialized memory.

This is entirely self inflicted as SGLang is optimized for (near) maximum performance. Another issue is that this is dealing with a device driver rather than system memory which rust has very little control over, as in there is no native implementation in rust that allows you to address multiple-memory buffers. Think how old games had 16 different memory blocks all starting at 0 since the cpu could only address 65 kilobytes.
